# SK3060 — The lock is entered and not released on every path

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `Monitor.Enter` or a `ReaderWriterLockSlim` enter call whose matching release is not inside a `finally`, so anything that throws in between leaves the lock held for the life of the process.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2222, S7131, S7133 |

## Why

The `lock` keyword compiles to `Monitor.Enter` followed by `try`/`finally` `Monitor.Exit`, and that pairing is the whole reason the keyword exists. Writing the two calls by hand and putting the release on the happy path means the first exception inside the critical section keeps the lock forever: the next thread to ask for it blocks, and the one after that, and the process deadlocks somewhere entirely unrelated to the throw. ⚠ **The failure has no diagnostic anywhere** — the exception propagates normally and the deadlock happens later, in another thread, in another file, so nothing connects the two.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Ledger {
    readonly object gate = new();

    int balance;

    public void Post(int amount) {
        Monitor.Enter(gate);
        balance = checked(balance + amount);   // throws, and the lock is never released
        Monitor.Exit(gate);
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Ledger {
    readonly object gate = new();

    int balance;

    public void Post(int amount) {
        Monitor.Enter(gate);
        try {
            balance = checked(balance + amount);
        } finally {
            Monitor.Exit(gate);
        }
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Fixless.** Wrapping the rest of the method in a `try` is one repair and replacing the pair with a `lock` statement is another, and they mean different things about what the method does with its own exceptions — an edit that guesses can swallow one the caller was meant to see, or widen the critical section across an I/O call. ⚠ **The `lock` keyword is out of scope by construction rather than by a guard.** `lock (x) { }` lowers to exactly `Monitor.Enter` plus `try`/`finally` `Monitor.Exit`, and it leaves no `Monitor.Enter` invocation in the syntax tree; the rule registers on invocation expressions only, so a `lock` statement can never reach it. The negative fixture pins that anyway, because "cannot happen" is a claim and an unasserted claim is worth nothing. ⚠ **Pairing is per enter *method*, not per type, and that is what buys the mismatched-release finding rather than a branch written for it.** `EnterWriteLock` released by `ExitReadLock` has no matching `ExitWriteLock` anywhere, so it is reported by the ordinary "no matching release" path, and the fact that the author did write *a* release in *a* `finally` never enters into it. Collapsing the three `ReaderWriterLockSlim` rows into "an `Exit*` call" would lose exactly that finding — and `ExitReadLock` on a write lock throws, so the lock is then held forever *and* the `finally` throws over whatever was propagating. ⚠ **Stated scope limit: `SemaphoreSlim` and `Mutex` are out.** `Wait`/`Release` and `WaitOne`/`ReleaseMutex` are the same *shape* and a different *fact* — a semaphore acquired in one method and released in another is how a semaphore is meant to be used, so a missing `finally` is not evidence of anything there. The negative fixture set records that rather than hiding it. ⚠ **Three escapes, each of them recall spent on precision knowingly.** A type that releases from a *different* member has an `Acquire()`/`Release()` protocol on purpose and no `finally` could span two members. A release inside a lambda or a local function silences the rule rather than counting as one, because where a delegate runs is not knowable here. And a **partial** type is declined outright where it would otherwise report: the walk that finds the release starts from the syntactic type declaration holding the enter, so it sees one part and not the others, and the parts are usually in different files. ⚠ That last escape was added after the shape was **tested rather than reasoned about** — a partial type with `Acquire()` in one part and `Release()` in the other produced a false positive, and the fixture that proves it is `a-protocol-split-across-partial-parts.cs`. Walking every `DeclaringSyntaxReference` instead would make the answer for one file depend on files the cache key does not name, which is what `scope: Compilation` costs and what this rule declines to pay for a shape this rare. ⚠ **The `finally` test is lexical and deliberately not a flow analysis.** The rule asks whether some matching release sits inside a `finally` of this body; it does not prove that `finally` guards this critical section. Anything stronger needs flow, and a wrong answer from a flow analysis is a finding on threading code that was correct — docs/plan/16 § R3's most expensive reading.
